idiom_name: Parser[T] per rule composed with ~, |, rep and ^^ (scala-parser-combinators)
implementation_notes: Scala's classic realization is parser combinators: one Parser[T] value per grammar rule, composed with ~ (sequence), | (ordered choice), rep (repetition) and ^^/map (semantic action), run with parse(rule, input); the library was part of the standard library, is now the community-maintained scala-parser-combinators module, and its README documents both its stability and its weaknesses (performance, minimal feature set, inflexible error reporting). What replaces the classic structure is composition: there is no parser object with per-rule methods, only parser values whose types carry the results. Prefer it when the grammar is small, the combinator style is familiar and Scala 2.12/2.13/3 portability matters; choose FastParse when performance or diagnostics dominate.
pitfalls: Combinator parsers backtrack by default: ordered choice plus rep can be exponential without packrat memoization, and a PEG-style ordering means an earlier alternative that succeeds but is not the intended one silently changes the parse.
scala-parser-combinators reports failures as a string with a position and no expected-set detail; production diagnostics need a custom error formatter or a switch to FastParse.
Rule values are initialized eagerly: recursive grammars need def (not val) or a forward reference, otherwise the construction cycle throws a NullPointerException at startup.

variants.name: FastParse 3 combinators
variants.idiom_name: def rule[$: P]: P[T] = P(...) with ~, |, .rep and Parsed results
variants.implementation_notes: FastParse is the modern Scala combinator library: rules are defs returning P[T], wrapped in P(...) so mutual recursion works and the parser gets a name for error messages, composed with ~, |, .rep and .!, and run with parse(input, rule(_)) returning Parsed.Success or Parsed.Failure; its documentation claims speed comparable to a hand-written parser, roughly 200x that of scala-parser-combinators, plus layered error reporting (msg, longMsg, aggregateMsg, trace()). Choose it when throughput and diagnostics matter and a macro-based dependency is acceptable.
pitfalls: P(...) is required around every rule def: without it, mutually recursive parsers fail to initialize and error messages lose the rule name.
The `$/` cut operator changes backtracking semantics deliberately - once passed, alternatives are committed - so cuts placed too early turn recoverable failures into hard ones.
